query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a thin, conformal high‐entropy alloy (HEA) interlayer at the W/Cu interfaces will overcome the phase separation and interfacial void formation that normally develop during high-temperature and irradiation exposure, thereby enhancing the composite’s thermal conductivity relative to the untreated form.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite consisting of discrete tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments embedded in a copper matrix that, when processed without modification, is prone to phase separation and interfacial void formation under high heat and irradiation.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin interlayer—using methods such as sputtering or chemical vapor deposition—composed of a refractory HEA (for example, a W–Ta–Cr–V system) at the interfaces between the W phase and the Cu matrix during processing.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied prior to final consolidation, and the composite is subsequently subjected to high-temperature exposures (up to ~1500 °C) and irradiation conditions (comparable to Ar+, He+, and D+ fluences used in fusion-relevant studies) representative of joints between plasma-facing tungsten components and copper-based cooling components.
generation.structural_mediator: A stable, nanostructured HEA interphase that acts as a graded transitional zone between the highly refractory W and the more ductile Cu.
generation.mechanism: The HEA interlayer reduces interfacial energy mismatches by promoting chemical and structural compatibility, which inhibits the nucleation of voids and minimizes phase separation. In doing so, it maintains continuous, low-resistance pathways for heat transfer even under cyclic thermal and irradiation stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under equivalent high-temperature and irradiation conditions, composites with the HEA interlayer are expected to show a more uniform and continuous microstructure at the interface, with significantly fewer voids and reduced phase separation. This results in improved thermal conductivity compared to untreated composites.
generation.baseline: Untreated W–Cu composites that exhibit clear phase separation and interfacial void formation under high-temperature heat treatment and irradiation, leading to degraded heat-transfer performance.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the intervention will depend on maintaining the continuity and stability of the HEA interlayer during prolonged thermal cycling and irradiation. Its benefits might diminish if the interlayer reacts adversely or destabilizes at irradiation doses beyond certain thresholds.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by the ability of multi-element interlayers in related refractory and HEA systems to improve stability and modify interfacial energies, the optimal HEA composition, precise interlayer thickness, and long-term behavior under combined heat and particle irradiation conditions remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites: one set deposited with a thin HEA interlayer (e.g., a sputter-deposited W–Ta–Cr–V layer) at the W/Cu interfaces and a control set without the interlayer. Process both sets under identical conditions. Subject each to high-temperature annealing (up to 1500 °C) and sequential irradiation (using Ar+, He+, and D+ ions at fluences comparable to fusion-relevant conditions). Post-exposure, conduct detailed microstructural and thermal characterizations.
measurements: Interfacial microstructure and void density via SEM/EDS and TEM
Phase identification and homogeneity via XRD
Thermal conductivity measurements (e.g., using laser flash analysis)
Evaluation of irradiation-induced swelling and structural degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the composites with the HEA interlayer do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in phase separation and interfacial voids, or if no improvement in thermal conductivity is observed relative to the control samples after high-temperature and irradiation exposure, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were produced by mechanical alloying and sintering and annealed at 1100 °C, 1300 °C, and 1500 °C. The irradiation resistance of the as-sintered materials was also evaluated. Therefore, the materials were irradiated with Ar+ (150 keV) with a fluence of 2.4 × 1020 at/m2, as well as He+ (10 keV) and D+ (5 keV), both with a fluence of 5 × 1021 at/m2. A very fine and homogeneous microstructure composed of three phases was observed in both as-sintered alloys. After annealing, considerable phase growth was observed. Both alloys presented three phases: a phase with a bcc-type structure, a hexagonal C14 Laves phase, and a Ti-rich oxide. These phases maintained their structure even after 8 days at 1500 °C, indicating high thermal stability. It was concluded that for the sample containing Cr, the bcc-type phase is a solid solution of W and Ta, while in the case of the sample containing V, it is a solid solution of W, Ta and V. In both alloys, the Laves phase is derived from Fe2Ta, in which Ta atoms are partially replaced by W atoms and the Fe atoms are partially replaced by Cr or V in the (CrFeTiTa)70W30 alloy and VFeTiTaW alloy, respectively.
